newsitem.title: USA: How Clinton pulled it off -- anatomy of a comeback.
newsitem.headline: How Clinton pulled it off -- anatomy of a comeback.

text.p: When President Bill Clinton gets around to sending out thank-you notes to the people who helped him win a second term, one of the recipients might well be Republican Newt Gingrich.

Clinton's aides believe the 1994 Republican takeover of Congress and Gingrich's elevation to the post of Speaker of the House of Representives set the stage for Clinton to rise from a political grave and become the first Democrat to be re-elected for 54 years.

"Newt Gingrich is the best friend the Democrats ever had. He pursued extreme policies using extreme politics, which focused the debate on what the Republicans wanted to do, where they wanted to take America, and the American people rejected that," Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart said.

There were other major factors in Clinton's re-election -- the strong U.S. economy, a relative calm in world affairs and Republican challenger Bob Dole's unfocused, zig-zagging effort to crown his long political career by winning the presidency.

Dole "reversed himself on all sorts of things he had previously stood for", like affirmative action to promote minorities and conservative fiscal policy, White House chief of staff Leon Panetta said in an interview.
"Had Dole been true to himself, I think he would have been a more competitive candidate," he said.

There was also Clinton's boundless zest for campaigning -- a prominent Democratic political consultant called him "the best since Bobby Kennedy" -- and his co-opting of Republican themes with a "family values" agenda crafted by Dick Morris, his gifted political strategist who was forced to quit late in the campaign in a sex scandal.

But Clinton's re-election was one of the marvels of modern American politics. It came just two years after his Democratic Party was repudiated by voters in the 1994 congressional elections as too consumed with taxing and spending.
In the weeks after that Clinton was at his weakest, at one news conference considering it necessary to point out that the president was still "relevant."

The Clinton camp to a person points to Gingrich's call at that time for a Republican "revolution" and his party's pursuit of an agenda many voters considered too extreme as the defining moment in Clinton's march back to victory.

The election led to a fierce budget battle between Clinton and the Republicans that twice shut the government. Gingrich, a conservative hardliner, led the fight for Republican proposals that Clinton said would have gutted popular health, education and enviromental programmes.

The speaker became highly unpopular because of his aggressive behaviour in the power struggle. He made himself the butt of ridicule when he said that his unyielding attitude stemmed in part from his poor seat assignment on the president's plane on a trip to Israel for Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin's funeral.

Dole, who was then preparing to challenge Clinton for the presidency, played second fiddle to the speaker in the Christmas-time budget fight, which dragged on for more than a month before Clinton finally prevailed.

"If Gingrich had understood that power is about compromising and doing things, I think it would have been a very different (presidential) race," Panetta said. "When the Republican Congress challenged us on the budget, and were willing to shut the government down to do it, it showed what they were about but also what Bill Clinton was about."
Echoing Panetta's comments, a top Democratic political strategist said the budget battle was "the seminal event" of the election campaign because it "redefined Clinton as a leader."

"People had previously considered him weak, but here he was standing firm on mainstream issues," the strategist said. "His advisers urged him to cut a deal, but he was steadfast in that confrontation."

A White House insider said that during one particularly tense budget negotiating session in the Oval Office, Clinton pointed to his desk and told Gingrich and Dole that for them to get what they wanted, "someone else will have to be sitting in that chair."

Gingrich's confrontational style also helped Clinton avoid internal opposition in the presidential primaries that might have split the Democratic party and softened him up for a kill in the general election.
"Our backs were to the wall. It made the Democrats realise that they couldn't engage in self-indulgent fratricide the way they usually do," a top aide to a leading Democratic senator told Reuters.

So Clinton was able to stay above the battle at a time when Dole was struggling to extinguish a Republican brushfire lit earlier this year by conservative Patrick Buchanan and by flat tax advocate Stephen Forbes -- a process that scarred Dole politically and left him broke financially.
In a move that went largely unnoticed in Washington, Clinton used his unspent primary campaign war-chest to saturate key states with television commercials.
"By staying up on the air, we set the agenda for this campaign. Dole never found a voice or an alternative message that could break through," Lockhart said.
